subchapters.title: External Features, Orientation, Borders, Surfaces & Chambers of the Human Heart

learning_objectives.statement: Describe the position of the heart in the middle mediastinum and its attitudinal (in-body) orientation, including apex, base, surfaces and borders.
Identify the four chambers and the external sulci (coronary, anterior and posterior interventricular) and relate them to the underlying chambers.
Explain which chambers form each border and surface seen on a PA chest radiograph.
Distinguish the anatomical "base" (posterior surface) from the inferior (diaphragmatic) surface.

prerequisites: Thoracic cage and mediastinal divisions (ANAT-001 general/thoracic orientation)
Basic cardiac embryology: heart tube looping (HIST-035)
key_concepts_and_terminology: Right, left, inferior and superior borders
clinical_applications: Cardiac silhouette on PA chest radiograph and what each border represents
Apex beat location and shifts in disease
Sites for percussion and auscultation relative to surface anatomy
Why anterior chest trauma most often involves the right ventricle
diagrams_models_and_practicals: Rotatable 3D heart with attitudinal orientation toggle (valentine vs in-body)
Labelled PA chest radiograph overlay
Dissection-style annotated photographs (license required)
Practical: surface marking of heart borders on a volunteer or manikin
assessment_objectives: Label the borders and surfaces on a diagram
Identify which chamber forms the right border and the apex
Short answer: describe the surface anatomy of the heart
Image-based question on a PA radiograph silhouette

subchapters.title: Pericardium: Fibrous & Serous Layers, Transverse & Oblique Pericardial Sinuses & Tamponade

learning_objectives.statement: Describe the fibrous and serous (parietal and visceral) pericardium, their attachments and nerve supply.
Locate the transverse and oblique pericardial sinuses and state their boundaries.
Explain the anatomical basis and clinical consequences of pericardial effusion and cardiac tamponade.
Identify landmarks used for pericardiocentesis and the structures at risk.

Pericardiocentesis approaches and structures at risk
Constrictive pericarditis
Use of the transverse sinus in cardiac surgery to clamp the great arteries

learning_objectives.statement: Describe the internal features of the right atrium (sinus venarum, pectinate muscles, crista terminalis, fossa ovalis, openings).
Describe the right ventricle inflow and outflow components, trabeculae carneae, papillary muscles and the septomarginal trabecula.
Identify the Triangle of Koch and state its boundaries.
Relate right-sided structures to common congenital and acquired lesions.

subchapters.title: Left Atrium & Left Ventricle: Pulmonary Venous Inflow, Aortic Vestibule & Wall Thickness Morphometry

learning_objectives.statement: Describe the internal features of the left atrium and left atrial appendage and the four pulmonary vein openings.
Describe the left ventricular inflow and outflow tracts, papillary muscles and the aortic vestibule.
Compare right and left ventricular wall thickness and explain the physiological reason.
Relate the posterior relations of the left atrium to the oesophagus and explain clinical consequences of left atrial enlargement.

subchapters.title: Fibrous Cardiac Skeleton, Atrioventricular (Tricuspid/Mitral) & Semilunar Valves: Mechanics & Auscultation

learning_objectives.statement: Describe the fibrous skeleton and its functions, including electrical insulation between atria and ventricles.
Describe the structure of the tricuspid, mitral, aortic and pulmonary valves, including cusps, chordae tendineae and papillary muscles.
Explain valve opening and closing in relation to the cardiac cycle.
State the surface projection and best auscultation sites of each valve and relate them to heart sounds.

Infective endocarditis predilection
Accessory pathways crossing the fibrous skeleton (pre-excitation)
